messages.body_plain:
Hello All,
Welcome to MAD 2.0! During our first meeting, we will welcome and introduce members of the community, and set some guidelines for participating in MAD in person and on our new online forum (mad.oxli.org <http://mad.oxli.org>).

Hope to see you there!

Time: 3:00pm-5:00pm
Location: 1043 Valley Hall room (http://campusmap.ucdavis.edu/?b=178).

Description

Meet and Analyze Data (MAD) is a community focused on tackling biological big data questions ranging from high level concepts (what is metagenome assembly?) to low level coding problems (what does this error message even mean!?) and everything in between. Each week will start with a short lesson to share important tools for project management and data analysis designed to help us level up our skills. Then, participants with expertise in a variety of areas will be available to help with individual research and coding questions. To facilitate this discussion, all questions must be posted on the MAD discourse forum <https://mad.oxli.org/>. Help us help you: please try to post your questions ahead of time, and be kind to our helpers as they try to get to all the questions! To keep things fun for everyone, please check out our Code of Conduct <http://ivory.idyll.org/lab/coc.html>.

Schedule
Date Topic
2-Oct MAD 2.0: how to help us help you Location: Valley Hall 1043
9-Oct What is the shell?
16-Oct Practical software management with conda, Pt 1
23-Oct no MAD
30-Oct Practical software management with conda, Pt 2
6-Nov Project organization and management
13-Nov How to backup data on a remote computer
20-Nov Quick sequencing data insights with sourmash
27-Nov Thanksgiving – no MAD
4-Dec Automation with Snakemake, Pt 1
11-Dec Automation with Snakemake, Pt 2

More info

https://dib-training.readthedocs.io/en/pub/#meet-and-analyze-data-mad

Best,
The DIB-lettes

What i want

"q.1",   "q.2",   "q.3",   "q.4",  "q.5"

Hello Balal,

For your first question, check out vroom, which is 50-60 times faster than read.delim():
> https://vroom.r-lib.org
>
For your second question, sprintf() returns a character vector rather than a single string.  You’ll need to use paste(), like so:
> foo = sprintf(“q.%s”, 1:5)
> paste(foo, collapse = “, “)
>
As an aside, note that 1:5 is already the vector of integers from 1 to 5. No need to wrap them in seq().  To create the same vector using seq(), you want seq(1, 5).

messages.body_plain:
Hi Elizabeth,

I think the issue is actually arising from using position = “dodge”. When you change to “dodge”, your bars are actually no longer stacked. Look at your data- for the year 2010, what is the highest value for “average”? If you total up the “average” values for 2010 Fails, will it be 200 or far more? I think your bars are actually getting layered one in front of the other within each year+pass.fail category, rather than stacked on top of each other.

If you do position = “stacked”, should stack correctly, but then Pass.Fail will be stacked on top of each other. One way around that is to use x = pass.fail , position = “stacked”, and facet.grid(~year) to put years side by side, with separate stacked bars for pass and fail.

I played with some dummy data to make these plots, take a look and see if they work for you:

library(tidyverse)

set.seed(51)
d <- tibble(year = rep(2012:2015, 5), average = sample(10:70, 20),
            pass_fail = sample(c("fail", "pass"), 20, replace = T))

# how tall should each bar be if we stack by year+pass_fail combination?
d %>%
  group_by(year, pass_fail)%>%
  summarise(sum(average))

# arrange data by descending average, and then plot with position = "dodge"
d %>%
  arrange(desc(average)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = average, fill = pass_fail, group = pass_fail)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", color = "black")
# take a look at 2012 fail the bar is like 69 tall, but according to our summary table it should be 195. the bars are getting placed one in front of the other, not stacked

# this should get the plot we want
d %>%
  arrange(desc(average)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = pass_fail, y = average, fill = pass_fail, group = pass_fail)) +
  geom_col(color = "black") +
  facet_grid(~year)

Hi Rachael,

There are a few things going on here:

- I believe the function you're looking to use is "lmer()", not "lme()"
- You need to explicitly specify your data within the function call (I'm going to assume your data frame is called "my_data_frame")
- If, as your random effects, you're looking to have varying intercepts by "Animal_ID", you'll need to specify those like so in your model formula: "(1|Animal_ID)"

Thus, I think this should work for you:

LA <- lmer(duration ~ Trt + TrialDay + Trt*Trialday + (1|Animal_ID), data = my_data_frame)

>From there, I'd recommend checking out the example code here: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/lme4/vignettes/lmer.pdf

All my best,
Evan

Hi Rachael (and everyone else),

The developer of lme4 explains why p-values aren’t reported here:
> https://stat.ethz.ch/pipermail/r-help/2006-May/094765.html
>
There’s a complementary explanation here:
> https://bbolker.github.io/mixedmodels-misc/glmmFAQ.html#testing-hypotheses
>
Both of these discussions are pretty technical — I’ll admit that I don’t fully understand them.  But, insofar as I do understand them, they argue that the error distributions for multilevel models are often much, much more complicated than the error distributions for plain linear regression (especially when they’re fit using REML rather than maximum likelihood).  Computationally simple ways of estimating errors are only really appropriate to special cases; more robust methods are computationally involved (and so take longer); and even the more robust methods can break in non-obvious ways.  So, in the spirit of fire season, it seems like there should be Red Flag warnings around any p-values reported from a multilevel model.

I don’t know the nlme package very well, so I don't know how it calculates p-values or how the authors of that package might respond to the arguments above.

If you do want to generate p-values or the like for lmer() models, the lme4 docs include this page, listing various methods:
> https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/lme4/versions/1.1-21/topics/pvalues
>
Cheers,
Dan

Dan, thanks for getting back to me. Your response prompted me to take a deeper dive into the survey package, which ultimately led me to the answer.

Both survey:svytotal() and srvyr::survey_total() were giving me similar SE results, until I specified the scale and rscale arguments. Once I did that, functions from both packages are giving me good-looking results.

Using the srvyr package
repweights = rep(paste0("PWGTP",1:80))

pumsd <- ppl_0_14 %>%
  as_survey_rep(
    variables = agegrp,
    weights = PWGTP,
    repweights = repweights,
    combined_weights = TRUE,
    mse =TRUE,
    type="other",
    scale=4/80,
    rscale=rep(1,80)
  )

# calculate pop and SE
  pumsd %>%
  group_by(agegrp) %>%
  summarise(
    count = survey_total())

Using the survey package

svydesigntst <-
survey::svrepdesign(data=ppl_0_14,
                    weights= ppl_0_14[,9],
                    repweights=ppl_0_14[,17:96],
                   combined.weights=TRUE,
                   type="other",
                   scale=4/80,
                   rscales=rep(1,80))

survey::svytotal(~agegrp, svydesigntst)

Subject: Reminder: #maptimeDavis Cloud Computing for Large Geospatial Datasets

Tuesday, October 22 from 10:00 AM - 12:00 PM in the DataLab Classroom, room 360 Shields Library, join #maptimeDavis and speaker Lauren Mabe for a workshop on cloud-based parallel computing!  The workshop will cover how to set up the parallel computing on a local computer and how to apply these skills to a cloud computing environment.  These skills are useful for speeding up processes like Monte Carlo analysis on large spatial datasets that would otherwise take a long time.

After this workshop learners should be able to:

– Understand the advantages of cloud computing

– Be able to set up and run a process in a cloud computing environment

– Identify additional resources

Prepare:  No previous experience is necessary.  Bring a laptop computer with R (and RStudio) installed.  You will also need the doParallel, sp, raster, and spData packages for R.

Meet and Analyze Data (MAD) is a community focused on tackling biological big data questions ranging from high level concepts (what is metagenome assembly?) to low level coding problems (what does this error message even mean!?) and everything in between.
